lines.text: Right now, there's a capable A.I. model sitting idle on a laptop in this room.
And someone who needs it can't reach it.
Local models are private and cheap to run. But they're stuck on one machine.
And when compute does get shared, nobody can say who used what, or what it cost.
So we built Open Compute Mesh.
Share compute. Run models. See every token.
Here's the whole thing, end to end, running for real.
You scan a QR code and join with a nickname. No account, no password.
To share compute, a small agent runs next to your local model. In Python, or as a single Rust binary.
It dials out to the coordinator. It never opens a port on your machine, and it only talks to your model on loopback.
You choose exactly which models to share, and you can pause or revoke at any time.
Now, pick a model that a real node is serving, and send a prompt.
The coordinator finds the least busy machine with that exact model, places a credit hold, and dispatches the job.
Tokens stream back over a WebSocket, live.
Then you get a receipt.
Input and output tokens, reported by the runtime itself. Time to first token. Model load, prompt evaluation, generation. Every millisecond, accounted for.
You pay the measured cost, and the owner earns exactly the same, in an append only ledger that's checked for balance.
Share the same model yourself, and you can race your machine against the network, side by side.
Underneath, every layer is pluggable.
Runtimes sit behind one adapter. Ollama runs locally, and a Gemini A.P.I. adapter plugs into the same interface, with token counts from Gemini's own usage data.
Every finished job flows into Tiger Data, as a Timescale D.B. hypertable. A continuous aggregate powers the live throughput chart.
And Sentry watches the coordinator, with scrubbers that strip prompts, outputs and secrets before anything leaves the machine.
This isn't a mock-up.
A Python coordinator, two agents, a React app, seventy-six tests, and C.I. on every push.
We ran it through a public tunnel, from a phone, and the receipts matched the runtime.
And we learned the hard way. Rust's T.L.S. stack panicked on our first secure connection, and a dishonest node taught us to cap every charge at the hold.
Open Compute Mesh. Bring the hardware you already own.
It's open source, on GitHub.
